    Recommender Systems · Chapter 3

    Personalized recommendation: content-based filtering

    This interactive course follows the slides of Chapter 3. Every section is one slide, with its yellow note, its figures and its formulas, plus simulators you can play with, exercises you can check, and questions that tell you if you understood. In Chapter 2 everybody saw the same list. Here, each user gets his own list.

    Problem

    Which movie should we recommend to User A?

    With popularity, User A would receive the same romantic comedy as every other user. Yet two pieces of information are available: the content of the movies (sci-fi, romance…) and User A's own ratings (sci-fi 5★, romance 1★). Combining them points to Dune. This is the principle of content-based filtering.
    User A rated…GenreRating
    InceptionSci-fi · Action5 ★
    InterstellarSci-fi · Drama5 ★
    The NotebookRomance · Drama1 ★
    CandidateGenrePopularity
    Notting HillRomance · Comedy#1
    The MartianSci-fi · Drama#14
    DuneSci-fi · Action#22

    Chapter 2 (popularity): User A receives “Notting Hill”, like every other user.

    Content-based answer: Dune or The Martian: their content is SIMILAR to the movies he rated highly, and different from the one he rated low.

    Which movie should be recommended to User A first?

    Key idea: use the CONTENT of the items and the ratings of THIS user → a personalized list.
    Problem statement

    The questions this chapter answers

    Five questions, five parts. Q2 and Q3 are the tools (vectors and similarity), Q4 assembles them into a working recommender, Q5 is the critical part: when does it fail? The summary slide at the end answers each question with a method and its limit.

    Common thread · 1/5

    From one list for everybody to one list per user

    The machinery is the same as in Chapter 2: compute a score, sort, show the Top-N. The only change: the score now depends on the pair (user, item). Two users = two scores for the same item = two different homepages.

    Chapter 2 · non-personalized

    score(item)Same Top-N for everybody: average, smoothing, popularity, PageRank.

    Chapter 3 · personalized

    score(user, item)A different Top-N for each user: content-based (this chapter), collaborative (next), hybrid.
    Common thread · 2/5

    What is a feature?

    A feature is simply a characteristic of the item, written as a number. Here we keep only 2: how much sci-fi and how much romance a movie contains, from 0 to 1. Inception = 0.9 sci-fi and 0.1 romance. With only 2 features we can draw every movie as a point on a graph (next slide).
    Feature = a characteristic that describes an item, measured by a number (here from 0 = not at all to 1 = completely).
    Moviex1 = Sci-fix2 = RomanceIn words
    Inception0.90.1very sci-fi, almost no romance
    Interstellar0.80.2sci-fi, a little romance
    The Notebook0.00.9no sci-fi, strong romance
    Dune0.80.0sci-fi, no romance
    The Martian0.70.1sci-fi, almost no romance
    Notting Hill0.10.8strong romance

    Book

    genre, author, pages

    Phone

    brand, price, screen size

    Song

    tempo, genre, energy
    Why only 2? We start with 2 features so that we can draw them (next section). Part 4 uses 5 features: same idea.
    Common thread · 3/5

    Everything becomes a vector

    Each movie is the point (sci-fi, romance) of the table. User A is placed in the same graph: the average of the two movies he rated 5★, so (0.85, 0.15), a sci-fi fan. The unseen movies whose arrow points in the same direction (The Martian, Dune) are recommended; Notting Hill points elsewhere.

    1 · Item = vector

    Each movie = its 2 features = a point. Inception = (0.9, 0.1)

    2 · User = vector

    Average of the movies he rated 5★: ((0.9 + 0.8)/2, (0.1 + 0.2)/2) = (0.85, 0.15)

    3 · Recommend = same direction

    The Martian 0.99 ✓ · Dune 0.98 ✓ · Notting Hill 0.29 ✗ (cosine, Part 3)

    Check: a User B gave 5★ to The Notebook (0, 0.9) and Notting Hill (0.1, 0.8).

    User B = ((0 + 0.1)/2, (0.9 + 0.8)/2) = (0.05, 0.85): a romance fan. Dune = (0.8, 0) points in a very different direction → no.

    Common thread · 4/5

    Four steps, always the same

    Steps 1 and 2 are data (features, ratings). Step 3 builds the taste profile of the user. Step 4 compares this profile with every item he has not seen and sorts. No other user is needed: this is the big difference with collaborative filtering (next chapter).

    1 · Item profiles

    describe each item with features

    2 · User ratings

    what did THIS user like?

    3 · User profile

    average of the items he liked

    4 · Similarity & sort

    cos(user, item) → Top-N
    Common thread · 5/5

    3 questions to ask on every section

    Same reading grid as Chapter 2. For content-based: DATA = item features + this user's ratings; SCORE = similarity between his profile and the item; LIMIT = needs good features, fails for a new user, keeps the user in his bubble.

    1 · DATA

    item features + this user's ratings

    2 · SCORE

    similarity: cos(profile, item)

    3 · LIMIT

    no features, new user, filter bubble

    Which data does content-based filtering need?

    01

    A good recommendation

    Four qualities, and two families of personalized recommender systems.

    Explanation

    What is a good recommendation?

    Relevant is not enough. Ten copies of the same type of movie are relevant but boring (not diverse). Recommending the fridge you bought last week is relevant but useless (not fresh). A product out of stock is relevant but frustrating (not available). A good RS balances the four.

    Personalized

    relevant to THAT userUser A rates sci-fi highly → Dune

    Diverse

    covers his different interestsnot 10 sci-fi movies in a row

    Fresh

    never the same item twiceno 2nd fridge after buying one

    Available

    can really be used or boughtin stock, in his country

    A shop recommends the same washing machine you bought last week. Which quality is violated?

    Explanation

    Personalized recommender systems

    Look at the arrows. Left (collaborative): the link goes through ANOTHER USER who read the same articles. Right (content-based): the link goes through the ARTICLE itself, which is similar to what the user read. This chapter is the right-hand picture.

    A personalized RS analyzes the user's data: purchases, ratings, and relationships with other users. Every user gets customized recommendations. The most popular types are:

    In one line: collaborative asks “who is like you?”. Content-based asks “what is like what you liked?”.
    Explanation

    Two families: who is similar, or what is similar?

    The key row is "data needed". Collaborative filtering never looks inside the items, it only knows who liked what. Content-based never looks at other users, it only knows the items' content and your own history. Each one is blind where the other sees.
    Collaborative filteringContent-based filtering
    QuestionWhich USERS are like you?Which ITEMS are like those you liked?
    Data neededratings of MANY usersitem features + YOUR ratings
    Knows the content?no (only who liked what)yes (genre, author, brand, text…)
    New item (0 rating)cannot recommend itcan recommend it at once
    Surprise / discoverygoodweak (similar items only)
    Example“Customers who bought this also bought…”“Because you watched Inception…”
    Exercise 1

    Collaborative or content-based?

    Method: ask "what data does the system read?". If it reads a description of the item (genre, keywords, image, author), it is content-based. If it reads what OTHER users did (bought, rated, watched), it is collaborative. One scenario is the typical strength of content-based.
    Your turn · classify the 6 scenarios
    Remember: scenario 4 shows the big strength of content-based: it can recommend an item nobody has rated yet.
    02

    Item profiles

    Describe every item with numbers: a feature vector.

    Explanation

    Content-based filtering: the idea

    The hypothesis is simple: you will like what resembles what you liked. If you bought a Samsung phone, maybe a Samsung watch. It works well when tastes are stable. But "resembles" must be computed, so we first need to describe the items with numbers.
    • Recommend to customer X items that are similar to his previously rated items.
    • The user's purchase history is observed.
    • Example: a user already read a book from one author, or bought a product of a certain brand → he probably prefers that author / brand → he may buy a similar product in the future.
    Explanation

    An item profile = a vector of features

    A feature can be binary (the actor plays in the series: 1 or 0) or a degree (0.9 action). Text values like "white" must be encoded into numbers. The golden rule: all items use the same features in the same order, otherwise position 2 means "romance" for one item and "price" for another.
    CatalogueFeatures (same order for every item)ExampleType
    Movies[action, romance, horror, fantasy, drama]Inception = (0.8, 0.1, 0, 0.3, 0.4)float
    Series[actor1, actor2, actor3, actor4, …]Series A = (1, 0, 1, 0)binary
    Home appliances[color, electric/manual, usage, size]Mixer = (white, 1, kitchen, small) → encodedmixed
    Worked example

    Our running example: the movie-profile table

    Read each row as a recipe: m1 is 90% action and 10% horror. m2 and m4 have almost the same recipe (romance + drama), so they should be very similar. Keep this table in mind: it is Step 1 of the pipeline of Part 4, and every computation of the chapter uses it.

    Just by looking, which two movies are the most alike?

    Explanation

    Where do the features come from?

    Metadata is easy but poor (two "comedies" can be very different). Text and images give much richer vectors but need NLP or deep learning: this is the TP. TF-IDF is the classic trick for text: a word that appears everywhere ("the") says nothing, a rare word ("wizard") says a lot.

    Metadata

    genre, author, brand, price, yeareasy, but poor

    Text

    keywords: TF-IDF, word embeddingsTP ex. 1 & 2

    Images

    a CNN turns a photo into a vectorTutorial 3 · TP ex. 3

    Tags / experts

    hand-made labelsprecise, but expensive
    Try it · TF-IDF on three short documents (change the texts!)
    What to notice: “magic” and “wizard” appear in 2 documents, so their idf is small; “school” or “romance” appear only in document 1, so they get a higher weight. Documents 1 and 3 (both fantasy) have the highest cosine. This is TP exercise 1.

    03

    Similarity measures

    Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, Pearson, Jaccard: five ways to say “these two are alike”.

    Vector toolkit

    Vector toolkit: the 3 operations you need

    Only three operations are needed in this chapter. Dot product: multiply position by position and add, it is large when both vectors are high on the SAME features. Norm: the length of the arrow, with Pythagoras. Cosine = dot product divided by the two norms.
    OperationIn wordsExample: A = (1, 2), B = (4, 6)
    Vectora list of numbers, one per featureA = (1, 2) · B = (4, 6)
    Dot product A·Bmultiply term by term, then add1×4 + 2×6 = 16
    Norm ||A||length of the arrow (Pythagoras)||A|| = √(1² + 2²) = √5 ≈ 2.24 · ||B|| = √52 ≈ 7.21

    Warm-up: A = (3, 4) and B = (2, 0).

    A·B = 3×2 + 4×0 = 6 · ||A|| = √(9 + 16) = 5 · ||B|| = √4 = 2 · cos = 6 / 10 = 0.6.

    Overview

    Similarity measures

    Two families in this table. Distances (Euclidean, Manhattan): 0 means identical, a large value means different. Similarities (cosine, Pearson, Jaccard): a large value means alike. Mixing them up is the classic bug: sorting a distance in descending order recommends the WORST items.

    Distances: small = similar

    Euclidean, Manhattan

    Similarities: large = similar

    Cosine, Pearson, Jaccard
    Measure 1

    Euclidean distance: the straight line

    It is the ruler distance between two points: Pythagoras with as many terms as features. Ali (1,2) and Sara (4,6) are at distance 5. Weakness: if one feature is a price in DH (0 to 10,000) and the others are 0 to 1, the price decides everything. Normalize the features first.
    Ali = (1, 2), Sara = (4, 6)
    differences: 1 − 4 = −3 ; 2 − 6 = −4
    squares: 9 + 16 = 25
    d(Ali, Sara) = √25 = 5
    Measure 2

    Manhattan distance: walking the streets

    In Manhattan you cannot cross a building: you walk along the streets, so you add the horizontal and vertical steps: 3 + 4 = 7 instead of the straight line 5. Without squares, one huge difference on a single feature weighs less than with Euclidean.
    |1 − 4| + |2 − 6| = 3 + 4
    d(Ali, Sara) = 7
    Euclidean = 5 (straight line) · Manhattan = 7 (along the streets)
    Measure 3

    Cosine similarity: the angle between tastes

    The cosine only looks at the DIRECTION of the arrows. Sara watches 3 times more movies than Ali, but in the same proportions: same direction, cos ≈ 0.99. That is why the cosine is the default measure of content-based RS: we compare tastes, not volumes.
    A·B = 16 ; ||A|| = 2.24 ; ||B|| = 7.21
    cos = 16 / 16.12 ≈ 0.99
    Comparison

    Distance or angle? Same users, two answers

    This is the key slide of Part 3. Euclidean says Omar is closer to Ali than Sara, because Omar's arrow ends nearby. But Omar prefers action and Ali prefers romance. The cosine looks at the angle and correctly finds that Sara has Ali's taste. For tastes: cosine.
    Try it · move the two arrows
    Try this: click “Ali vs Sara” then “Ali vs Omar”. Euclidean says Omar is closer (3.16 < 5), the cosine says Sara has Ali's taste (0.99 > 0.65). Then put A = (0, 0): the cosine becomes undefined. That is exactly the user cold start of Part 5.
    Measure 4

    Pearson correlation: cosine after removing the mean

    Some people give 5★ easily, others never more than 3★. Pearson first subtracts each person's mean, then computes a cosine. U (5,4,2,1) and V (3,2,1,0) look different, but they rank the movies in the same order: Pearson ≈ 0.99. It goes from −1 (opposite) to +1.
    U (generous) = (5, 4, 2, 1), mean 3
    V (strict) = (3, 2, 1, 0), mean 1.5
    centered U = (2, 1, −1, −2)
    centered V = (1.5, 0.5, −0.5, −1.5)
    numerator = 3 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 7
    denominator = √10 · √5 ≈ 7.07
    Pearson ≈ 0.99
    Measure 5

    Jaccard similarity: overlap of two sets

    For yes/no data, count what the two items share and divide by everything they have together. 2 common tags out of 5 different tags = 0.4. Simple and readable, but blind to intensity: a tag "slightly romantic" counts as much as "very romantic".

    J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|

    number of common elements / number of elements in total0 = nothing in common · 1 = identical sets
    A = {fantasy, magic, adventure}
    B = {fantasy, adventure, romance, war}
    A ∩ B = {fantasy, adventure} → 2
    A ∪ B → 5 elements
    J(A, B) = 2 / 5 = 0.4
    Summary of Part 3

    Which measure should I use?

    There is no best measure in general, only a best measure for your data. Tastes and texts: cosine. People with different rating habits: Pearson. Tags and sets: Jaccard. Physical quantities on the same scale: Euclidean or Manhattan. To turn a distance into a similarity: 1/(1 + d).
    My data looks like…UseRangeSimilar when…
    degrees / counts / text vectors (tastes)Cosine0 → 1 (≥ 0 data)large
    ratings of people with different habitsPearson−1 → 1large
    yes / no, tags, setsJaccard0 → 1large
    physical quantities, same scaleEuclidean0 → ∞small
    same, robust to one big differenceManhattan0 → ∞small

    Distance → similarity: sim = 1 / (1 + d).

    Exercise 4

    Who has the same taste as u?

    u and v watch the same genres (sci-fi and action), v just watches 3 times more. w watches romance, which u never watched. Before computing, guess the answer. Then check which measure agrees with your common sense.

    Features [sci-fi, action, romance] = number of movies watched. u = (1, 1, 0) · v = (3, 3, 0) · w = (1, 0, 1)

    d(u, v) = √8 ≈ 2.83 ; d(u, w) = √2 ≈ 1.41 → Euclidean says w. cos(u, v) = 6 / (√2·√18) = 1 ; cos(u, w) = 1 / 2 = 0.5 → cosine says v. v likes exactly what u likes, he just watches 3× more: the cosine is right, Euclidean is fooled by the volume.

    04

    The content-based pipeline

    Item profiles + user ratings → user profile → cosine → prediction.

    Explanation

    Content-based RS with ratings: the full pipeline

    This picture is the heart of the chapter. Step 1: describe the movies. Step 2: collect the ratings. Step 3: turn each user into a taste vector in the same feature space. Step 4: compare with the cosine. The next slides compute each step by hand.

    In addition to “item properties”, it also uses “users' ratings of items” to recommend to customer X items similar to those rated highly by X:

    1 · Item profiles

    2 · User ratings

    3 · User profile = weighted average

    4 · Cosine → predict

    Step 1 of 4

    Step 1: describe each movie with 5 features

    Each movie gets one number per feature, between 0 and 1: how much action, romance, horror, fantasy, drama it contains. Read a row as a recipe: m1 is 90% action and 10% horror. In the formulas, xk(mj) means "feature k of movie j": x1(m1) = 0.9, x4(m3) = 0.5.

    What it means

    Each movie gets 5 numbers (0 to 1): HOW MUCH action, romance, horror, fantasy, drama it contains.m1 = (0.9, 0, 0.1, 0, 0) → 90% action, 10% horror.

    Notation

    xk(mj) = value of feature k for movie j: x1(m1) = 0.9, x4(m3) = 0.5

    x2(m4) = 0.7 (row m4, column x2) · x1(m3) = 0.4 · m3 has x4 fantasy = 0.5, the largest fantasy value.

    Step 2 of 4

    Step 2: collect the ratings of each user

    Now read the green table by COLUMN: each column is one user. u1 gave 5★ to m1 and m2. A "?" means he has not seen the movie: these are the ratings we want to predict. A 0 means he saw it and gave the lowest rating. In the formulas, ui(mj) means "rating of user i for movie j".

    What it means

    Read by COLUMN: one column = one user, his ratings of the 4 movies (0 to 5★).? = not seen → the rating to PREDICT · 0 = seen, lowest rating

    Notation

    ui(mj) = rating of user i for movie j: u3(m4) = 5

    u1(m2) = 5 · u4(m3) = 2 · three “?”: u1-m3, u2-m2, u2-m4.

    Step 3 of 4

    Step 3: turn the ratings into a user profile

    This step builds the taste of each user in the SAME 5 features as the movies. For one feature: multiply each rating by the value of that feature in the movie, add, divide by 4. A movie rated 5★ gives a lot of its features to the user, a movie rated 0 gives nothing. Reading tip: on each line read ui(mj), the ratings of user i.

    The formula in 3 moves (user i, feature k)

    ① multiply: rating ui(mj) × feature xk(mj), for each movie j② add the 4 products③ divide by 4 (number of movies) · “?” counts as 0
    Step 3 · worked example

    Step 3 in detail: the profile of u1

    Follow one line at a time. For action: u1 gave 5★ to m1 (0.9 action) and 5★ to m2 (0.1 action), so 5×0.9 + 5×0.1 = 5, divided by 4 = 1.25. The ? and the 0 add nothing. Result: u1 = (1.25, 0.875, 0.125, 0, 0.25): he likes action and romance, which matches the two movies he rated 5★.

    u1's ratings: m1 = 5, m2 = 5, m3 = ? (→ 0), m4 = 0

    Feature5×xk(m1) + 5×xk(m2) + 0×xk(m3) + 0×xk(m4)Sum÷ 4
    x1 action5×0.9 + 5×0.1 + 0×0.4 + 0×0.05.01.25
    x2 romance5×0.0 + 5×0.7 + 0×0.1 + 0×0.73.50.875
    x3 horror5×0.1 + 5×0.0 + 0×0.0 + 0×0.00.50.125
    x4 fantasy5×0.0 + 5×0.0 + 0×0.5 + 0×0.00.00
    x5 drama5×0.0 + 5×0.2 + 0×0.0 + 0×0.31.00.25

    Same computation for u2, u3, u4 gives the user-feature preference matrix:

    featureu1u2u3u4
    x1 action1.251.530.050.20
    x2 romance0.880.101.230.58
    x3 horror0.130.130.000.00
    x4 fantasy0.000.500.000.25
    x5 drama0.250.000.480.23
    Step 4 of 4

    Predict with the cosine: u2 and m2

    u2 likes action and fantasy; m2 is romance and drama. They share almost nothing: the dot product is small (0.22) and the cosine is 0.19, an angle of about 79°. Prediction: u2 will probably not like m2. The method agrees with common sense, and now it is a number.
    u2 = (1.525, 0.10, 0.125, 0.50, 0)
    m2 = (0.1, 0.7, 0, 0, 0.2)
    u2·m2 = 0.1525 + 0.07 = 0.2225
    ||u2|| ≈ 1.613 ; ||m2|| ≈ 0.735
    cos ≈ 0.19 → θ ≈ 79°: u2 will probably NOT like m2
    Simulator

    All predictions: who gets which movie?

    First check that the method is sane: the movies a user rated 5★ get a high cosine with his profile (u2-m1 0.95, u3-m4 1.00). Then read the 3 red "?": u1 should rather like m3 (0.58), u2 should not get m2 (0.19) nor m4 (0.06).
    Try it · the whole pipeline, live
    Try this: (1) click the cell u2 / m2 to see the computation of the slide. (2) Change u2's rating of m1 from 5 to 0: his profile loses its action, and the ranking changes. (3) Switch to “Centered ratings”: bad ratings now push features DOWN (red values): the method finally learns what a user rates low.
    Critical reading

    Four things to know about this method

    The method is simple but has hidden hypotheses. An unseen movie counts like a 0★ rating, and a bad rating never lowers a feature: centering the ratings fixes this. Dividing by 4 changes nothing for the cosine. And a cosine of 0.19 is a similarity, not a number of stars.

    “?” counts as 0

    An unseen movie weighs like a 0★ rating, and a bad rating never pushes a feature DOWN. Fix: center the ratings (rating − user mean).

    The 1/4 does not matter

    Dividing a vector by 4 changes its length, not its direction: the cosine is the same.

    cos is not a rating

    0.19 is a similarity, not stars. Either rank by cos, or use a convention (e.g. 5 × cos ≈ 1★).

    Only one user's data

    Strength: works alone. Weakness: never learns from others → little discovery.

    Reading the original formula: on each line of the Step 3 formula, read ui(mj) (the ratings of user i), and the sum runs over the 4 movies of the example.

    Features (binary, in this order): [Fantasy, Romance, Science].

    BookDescriptionLina
    b1A fantasy romance between a witch and a knight4 ★
    b2A dragon saga in a magic kingdom5 ★
    b3A physics textbook for beginners1 ★
    b4A romance between two astronauts on Mars?

    Step 1: b1 = (1,1,0) · b2 = (1,0,0) · b3 = (0,0,1) · b4 = (0,1,1) · b5 = (1,0,1). Step 2: predict b4 and b5 (counted 0).

    Step 3: Fantasy = (4 + 5)/5 = 1.8 · Romance = 4/5 = 0.8 · Science = 1/5 = 0.2 → Lina = (1.8, 0.8, 0.2).

    Step 4: ||Lina|| = √3.92 ≈ 1.98 ; ||b4|| = ||b5|| = √2 ≈ 1.414 ; denominator ≈ 2.80. Lina·b4 = 0.8 + 0.2 = 1.0 → 0.36 · Lina·b5 = 1.8 + 0.2 = 2.0 → 0.71 → recommend b5.

    Exercise 6

    A new user rated two movies

    Only two ratings: m1 (action, 4★) and m4 (romance + drama, 5★). Build the profile with the Step 3 formula: the unseen movies count as 0. Then compare the profile with m2 and m3. Before computing, guess: m2 resembles m4, which u5 liked most.

    u5 rated m1 = 4 and m4 = 5 (m2, m3 unseen). Data: ||m2|| ≈ 0.735, ||m3|| ≈ 0.648. Use the movie table above.

    u5 = (4·0.9/4, 5·0.7/4, 4·0.1/4, 0, 5·0.3/4) = (0.9, 0.875, 0.1, 0, 0.375) ; ||u5|| = √(0.81 + 0.766 + 0.01 + 0.141) ≈ 1.315.

    cos(u5, m2) = (0.09 + 0.6125 + 0.075) / (1.315 × 0.735) ≈ 0.80 ; cos(u5, m3) = (0.36 + 0.0875) / (1.315 × 0.648) ≈ 0.53 → recommend m2.

    Exercise 7

    A brand-new movie arrives

    m5 has no rating at all: nobody has seen it. But we know its content (romance, fantasy, drama), so it is a vector like the others. Compare it with the 4 user profiles and send it to the closest ones. Ask yourself: could collaborative filtering do the same?

    m5 = (0, 0.5, 0, 0.6, 0.2), no rating at all. ||m5|| ≈ 0.806. User norms: 1.551, 1.613, 1.315, 0.696.

    u1·m5 = 0.875·0.5 + 0.25·0.2 = 0.488 → 0.39 · u2·m5 = 0.10·0.5 + 0.50·0.6 = 0.35 → 0.27 · u3·m5 = 1.225·0.5 + 0.475·0.2 = 0.708 → 0.67 · u4·m5 = 0.575·0.5 + 0.25·0.6 + 0.225·0.2 = 0.483 → 0.86. Send it to u4 first. Collaborative filtering could not: m5 has no rating. No item cold start.

    Try it · design the new movie m5
    05

    Advantages and limits

    Cold start, filter bubble, sparsity, long tail… and how to fix them.

    Explanation

    Advantages and drawbacks of content-based RS

    Remember the asymmetry. A new ITEM is no problem: its features are enough (Exercise 7). A new USER is a big problem: with no rating, his profile is a zero vector and the cosine is not even defined (division by 0). The fix is to ask a few preferences at sign-up.

    Advantages

    • No item cold-start problem
    • Recommends items before any user tries them
    • Recommendations for one user do not depend on other users
    • Recommends unpopular (niche) products

    Drawbacks

    • Item information is necessary (good features)
    • User cold-start problem: not enough information to build a user profile → no recommendation
    Explanation

    Disadvantages of the content-based approach

    All five drawbacks have one root: content-based only looks at what you already liked. So it needs a lot of your data, it keeps you in your interests (bubble), and it rarely surprises you. It also depends on the quality of the item descriptions (sparsity).
    Filter bubblea user reads a book about a political ideology → only that ideology is recommended: he stays in the “bubble of his previous interests”
    Lots of user dataa lot of data about the user and his preferences must be collected
    Sparsityinsufficient data to extract descriptive metadata and ratings about items
    20 / 8020% of items attract 70–80% of the users' attention
    Little discoveryintroducing products the user would not find at first glance is achieved less well than with collaborative filtering
    Simulator

    The filter bubble

    The loop: you read sci-fi → the system shows sci-fi → you read sci-fi... For movies it is boring; for news and politics it can polarize people. Remedies: impose diversity in the list, add a little exploration (random or popular items), or mix with collaborative filtering.

    Diversity

    force several categories in the Top-N

    Exploration

    add a random or popular item from time to time

    Hybrid

    mix with collaborative filtering (next chapter)
    Try it · trapped in the bubble?
    Try this: run with ε = 0: the user never sees comedy, so the system never learns he likes it. Then ε = 0.2: comedy appears by chance and enters his profile. Then tick the diversity rule: his list finally contains both genres.
    Illustration

    The long tail: 20% of items, 80% of attention

    Most catalogues look like this: a few hits and a huge tail of rarely seen items. Content-based can recommend a tail item without any rating, as long as it matches your profile. But it only finds tail items SIMILAR to your past: it helps niche items be found, not users discover new tastes.
    Comparison

    Content-based vs collaborative vs popularity

    Read the table by row. New user: only popularity works. New item: only content-based works. Discovery: collaborative is best. No method wins every row, so real systems combine them: popularity for a new user, then content-based and collaborative once data arrives.
    Popularity (Ch. 2)Content-based (Ch. 3)Collaborative (Ch. 4)
    Personalized?noyesyes
    New userworksfailsfails
    New itemnever shownworksfails
    Discoverynoneweakgood
    Data neededcountsitem features + user's ratingsratings of many users
    Exercise 8

    Diagnose the problem

    For each situation, first ask: is the problem about the USER (not enough ratings), the ITEMS (not enough description), or the RESULT (too similar, no surprise)? Then pick the remedy. Careful: one of the five situations is actually a strength of content-based filtering.

    Tutorials & TP

    Tutorial implementation of a content-based RS: three notebooks, project ideas, and the TP to hand in.

    Tutorial 1

    Building a Simple Content-Based Recommender System

    This notebook is Parts 2 and 3 in code: each item description becomes a vector, then the cosine between items gives the most similar ones. Try to change one item description and see how its neighbours change.
    Scan to open the notebook (Google Colab). Steps: item descriptions → vectors → cosine between items → Top-N.
    Tutorial 2

    Content-based RS and Evaluating Accuracy Metrics

    A recommender must be evaluated: hide some ratings, predict them, compare with the truth. This notebook does exactly that for a content-based model. It is the scientific version of our check "movies rated 5★ get a high cosine".
    Scan to open the notebook. Steps: build the model → predict for test users → measure the accuracy.
    Tutorial 3

    Visual Content Similarity-based RS

    Here the features come from the images: a pretrained neural network turns each picture into a long vector of numbers. Two products that look alike get close vectors, and the cosine finds them. Same pipeline as the course, only the source of the features changes.
    Scan to open the notebook. Steps: pretrained CNN → image vectors → similarity → visually similar items.
    Projects

    Ideas for a visual-similarity project

    Each idea follows the same workflow as tutorial 3: collect images (and text), extract a vector per item, compute similarities, recommend the closest items. The best projects combine image features with another source (text, ratings): that is a hybrid system.

    1Artworkartwork images; VGG or Inception features; distance metrics
    2Recipesrecipe images + ingredients; CNN + NLP

    TP et rendus

    TP et rendus: the 7 exercises

    Exercise 1 is the direct application of the course: TF-IDF vectors (Part 2) + cosine (Part 3). Exercise 2 replaces TF-IDF by embeddings. Exercise 3 uses the images, like tutorial 3. Exercise 4 combines text and image scores: a first hybrid system.
    Exercice 1TF-IDF and Cosine Similarity: implement a content-based RS using TF-IDF for text features such as product titles and descriptions. Use cosine similarity to measure similarity between products.
    Exercice 2Word Embeddings: instead of TF-IDF, use word embeddings like Word2Vec or GloVe to represent text features. Compare the results with TF-IDF.
    Exercice 3Image Classification Model: build an image classification model (e.g. a CNN) to classify products into categories (men, women, boys, girls). Then recommend products from the same category.
    Exercice 4Hybrid Recommender System: combine text-based and image-based recommendations: ensemble approach or weighted average of the two scores.
    Exercice 5Matrix Factorization: implement SVD or ALS on the user-product interaction matrix to make personalized recommendations.
    Exercice 6Deep Learning Model: build a deep learning model (e.g. neural collaborative filtering) for content-based recommendations, with embeddings for user and product features, incorporating image and text information.
    Exercice 7Feature Engineering: experiment with different features or combinations of features, e.g. color information from images or product categories.
    Link with the course: Ex. 1 = Part 2 (TF-IDF simulator) + Part 3 (cosine). Ex. 3 = tutorial 3. Ex. 4 = Part 5 (hybrid). Ex. 5 and 6 prepare the next chapters.

    Summary & final quiz

    Back to the five questions of the chapter, then ten questions to check yourself.

    Summary

    Back to our questions: what we learned

    Content-based filtering = item vectors + a user vector built from his own ratings + the cosine. Its strength: new items and independence from other users. Its weakness: new users and the bubble. The next chapter uses other users to fix this: collaborative filtering.
